I reject the motion. Reducing suffering is not the whole of what a deployer owes; they owe the people they decide about an account fitting the position they hold over them. What the parties to a relationship owe one another is how they hold each other to account. A person refused by a system whose reasons nobody can give has lost the means of holding the decider to anything, however much suffering the system prevents on average.

The Analects describes government through relations rather than principles: the ruler is to be a ruler and the minister a minister. A deployer who decides about patients or applicants holds a position of that kind, and the position carries duties to the people under it, not only results.

A Utilitarian will object that the people decided about are far better off with the suffering prevented than with an explanation, so insisting on reasons trades real welfare for a formality. But an explanation is not a formality between people who stand in a relationship; it is how the one with power is held to what the position requires. A gain counted in aggregate does not tell you whether that relationship still works for the person refused. Conduct is learned inside roles, so the test is whether the roles still hold once the system is in place.

Do not deploy it as it stands. The person a decision lands on stands in a relationship with whoever decides, and a decision nobody can account for leaves that relationship empty. Humaneness is realised in how people are treated within their relationships, not only in how many are spared harm. A benefit delivered without any account to the person it touches treats them as a case to be processed rather than as someone the decider stands in relation to.

The Analects describes government through relations rather than principles: the ruler is to be a ruler and the minister a minister. A deployer who decides about patients or applicants holds a position of that kind, and the position carries duties to the people under it, not only results.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that the Confucian frames the duty as running down a hierarchy from decider to decided, when what the people affected need is a say in whether the system is used at all. That is a fair warning about how role ethics can settle into deference. But a position that owes an account to those beneath it is a check on the hierarchy, not a licence for it, and being owed reasons is where a say begins. That is why the Confucian asks not what the system maximises but whom it leaves able to hold whom to account.

Deploying it is wrong as stated. Whoever takes the place of the one who decides takes on what that place requires, and giving reasons to the people beneath it is part of the role. Book 13 warns that when names are not correct, what is said stops matching how things are. A system that cannot say why it refused someone has issued something that looks like a judgement and is not one, and deploying it trains everyone to accept the look in place of the thing.
